prompt:
Write an essay of about 800 words on the subject below.

Write it the way an excellent, idiosyncratic human essayist would: someone with real expertise and strong opinions, writing in the first person for their own blog. Commit to a specific thesis that a thoughtful reader might disagree with. Use concrete particulars (names, numbers, incidents, things only someone who had done the work would know) in place of general statements. Vary sentence length. No headings, no bullet points, no summary paragraph at the end, and none of the stock phrases of AI writing.

Output only the essay, with no title.

Subject: an essay explaining how public-key cryptography works
raw:
For about six years I've explained public-key cryptography to people who didn't ask: undergraduates, a roommate's father who ran a dental practice, a woman next to me on a delayed flight out of Denver. My view now is that the standard explanation, the one with the padlock, does more harm than the math it's trying to spare people. The padlock should be retired. The real ideas are smaller and stranger than the metaphor, and anyone who can do long division can follow them.

The padlock story goes like this. I mail you an open padlock. You put your message in a box, snap my lock shut, and mail the box back. Only I have the key, so only I can open it. Everyone nods. The trouble is that nobody leaves the story knowing anything they didn't already know. Everyone has seen a padlock you can close without a key, so the story makes the result sound obvious. What actually happened in the 1970s is that people found a mathematical operation that is easy in one direction and miserable in the other, plus a hidden shortcut that makes the miserable direction easy again. That shortcut is the entire trick, and the padlock hides it.

So here is what I do instead. Take two primes, 61 and 53. Multiply them and you get 3233. That multiplication takes a fourth-grader a minute. Now hand a stranger 3233 and ask which two primes produced it. They'll be trying divisors for a while. At four digits it's a chore. At six hundred digits, nobody on Earth can do it. The best published effort, RSA-250, took roughly 2,700 core-years of computing in 2020, and that number had only 250 digits.

From 61 and 53 you also compute a second number, (61−1)×(53−1), which is 3120. Only someone who knows the two primes can calculate it easily. Pick an exponent that shares no factors with 3120, say 17. Then find the number that undoes it, the d where 17 × d leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 3120. That's 2753. You publish 3233 and 17. You keep 2753 to yourself.

If I want to send you the number 65, I raise it to the 17th power and keep only the remainder after dividing by 3233. That gives 2790. Anyone watching the wire sees 2790. You raise 2790 to the 2753rd power, take the remainder mod 3233 again, and 65 comes back. I've watched people do this on a laptop calculator and get visibly annoyed that it works. That annoyance is the right response, and the padlock never produces it.

What the arithmetic makes clear is that the private key isn't some separate object that happens to fit the lock. It is knowledge of how the public number was built. The public key is a product, and the private key is its factors, in disguise. That idea is so simple it unsettles people, and it should.

My more contrarian claim is that we teach the history in the wrong order. RSA, from Rivest, Shamir and Adleman in 1977, gets the fame partly because Martin Gardner ran it in Scientific American that August and offered a challenge that went unsolved until 1994, when about 1,600 volunteer computers recovered the message "The Magic Words are Squeamish Ossifrage." But the conceptual break came a year earlier. Diffie and Hellman's "New Directions in Cryptography" showed that two people could agree on a secret over a channel where everything is overheard. Take the prime 23 and the base 5. I pick 6 in secret and send you 5⁶ mod 23, which is 8. You pick 15 and send me 5¹⁵ mod 23, which is 19. I compute 19⁶ mod 23 and get 2. You compute 8¹⁵ mod 23 and also get 2. The eavesdropper has 23, 5, 8 and 19 and cannot easily get to 2. Nothing was locked and nothing was mailed back. Two strangers ended up holding the same number. That is the thing that should amaze people, and it's what your browser does dozens of times an hour.

Then there's the part that every explanation skips, which is also the part that actually fails. The math is fine. The problem is knowing whose public key you're holding. If someone in the middle hands each of us their own key, we will both encrypt very carefully, straight to them. In 2011 a Dutch certificate authority called DigiNotar was breached, and forged certificates for google.com were used against roughly 300,000 users, mostly in Iran. No prime was factored and no exponent was broken. Someone simply vouched for the wrong key. The old PGP crowd understood this, which is why they held key-signing parties where people stood in hotel conference rooms reading hexadecimal fingerprints aloud and checking passports. It looked absurd, and it was the most honest picture of the problem anyone has managed.

One more detail I always save for the end. A GCHQ mathematician named Clifford Cocks came up with essentially RSA in 1973, reportedly in about half an hour, after his colleague James Ellis had described the idea of "non-secret encryption." It stayed classified until 1997. I like that story because it shows the idea was sitting there waiting, small enough for one person to work out between lunch and tea. The padlock makes it seem like engineering. It's really a remainder after division, and that's the version people should be taught.
